subject: business-studies

moments.title: Toyota Motor Co. founded
moments.body: Toyota begins as a spin-off from Toyoda Automatic Loom Works. The family name had used a 't' (Toyoda) — the new company chose 'Toyota' for fewer brushstrokes and clearer pronunciation.
moments.takeaway: Toyota's later innovations grew from a textile company's deep familiarity with autonomous machinery (jidoka — machines that stop when something goes wrong).

moments.title: Taiichi Ohno develops the Toyota Production System
moments.body: After WWII, Toyota cannot afford Detroit-style mass production. Ohno develops a system designed around small batches, fast changeovers, defect elimination, and worker problem-solving. Just-in-time inventory, kanban cards, andon cords (workers can stop the line) all emerge. The model is partly inspired by US supermarkets — replenishing shelves only when items are taken.

quote.text: Costs do not exist to be calculated. Costs exist to be reduced.

moments.takeaway: TPS turns Fordism inside out: instead of large buffers absorbing problems, problems must be visible and fixed immediately.

moments.title: The Machine That Changed the World
moments.who: James Womack, Daniel Jones and Daniel Roos, MIT International Motor Vehicle Program
moments.body: The MIT study compares automotive plants worldwide and finds Japanese 'lean' producers dramatically outperform Western mass producers on productivity, quality and inventory. The book popularises 'lean production' as a term and makes Toyota the global benchmark.
moments.takeaway: Lean spreads beyond automotive — into electronics, healthcare, software (lean startup, agile).

now.title: Lean as orthodoxy and its critics
now.body: Lean is now standard taught content in operations management. Variants include Lean Six Sigma, lean startup (Eric Ries, 2011), lean healthcare. Critics note that lean intensifies work (less buffer = more pressure) and that JIT supply chains are fragile to shocks (Fukushima 2011, semiconductor shortages, COVID).
now.open_questions: Can lean coexist with resilience? Toyota itself emphasises long-term supplier relationships and risk management — but the 'lean' label has often been applied more aggressively elsewhere.

reflection: A post-war Japanese carmaker, working under cash constraints, invented a system that became the global standard. Constraint isn't only a problem — sometimes it's the source of better ideas.
